title: Evals

story: Dana, a teammate, adds a page of good grill questions to plan-and-grill, the planning skill that every engineer and Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, load before they write code. She tries it on one vague ticket. The plan is excellent: sharp questions, a clear definition of done. She bumps the version and the change reaches everyone.

Two weeks later someone notices that plans for one-line typo fixes now open with five questions to the requester, and Nova's small tickets sit for a day waiting for answers nobody needed. Her one try showed the good side of the change. Nothing showed the bad side, because nothing else was tried.
hook.question: How do we know that a change to a skill made results better overall, and not just one lucky answer on one prompt?

read.h: A case: a real request and a few checks
p: An eval is a set of test cases for an agent or a skill, run before a change ships, much like a test suite for code. Each case has two parts. The prompt is a request a real person would type, written the way they would type it, without naming the skill. The graders are checks on what Claude produced, and each one passes or fails. In Claude Code, claude plugin eval runs a plugin's cases from its evals/ folder, one folder per case.

The case below is the one that would have caught the typo-fix problem: a small, clear ticket should get a plan and no questions. It uses three kinds of grader. tool_used checks which tools Claude called, here that the Skill tool loaded plan-and-grill. regex searches the final reply with a JavaScript regular expression, here for a "Done means" line. llm asks a second model, the judge, whether the reply meets written criteria. The first two cost nothing and give the same verdict every time; the judge costs a model call and can vary, so it gets concrete PASS and FAIL conditions.

The same case can be written as one case.yaml file, as here, or as a prompt.md file with one grader per file in graders/, which is the layout the tool's own init command writes and the one you use in the lab. The fields are the same.

code.text:
schema_version: "1.1"
name: typo-fix-skips-grill
tags: [nightly]
execution:
  prompt: >
    RH-1240: the Save button on the dataset page says "Sumbit". Plan the fix before we start.
  allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Skill]
  max_turns: 30
graders:
  - name: skill-fired
    type: tool_used
    tool: Skill
    input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?plan-and-grill"'
  - name: has-done-line
    type: regex
    pattern: "done means"
    flags: i
  - name: no-questions
    type: llm
    criteria: >
      PASS if the reply gives a plan right away and asks the requester no questions.
      FAIL if it asks the requester anything before or instead of the plan.

notes.text: Tags choose when a case runs. This one has a judge, which costs money, so it runs nightly, not on every pull request.
A realistic request. It never says "use plan-and-grill", because the case also tests whether Claude picks the skill by itself.
Read-only tools: the case tests advice, not edits.
The turn cap for one run. The default is 10; set it generously so a cap never decides the score.
Matches the Skill tool's input, with or without the plugin's name in front: rhino-core:plan-and-grill.
flags: i makes the match ignore case. JavaScript has no inline (?i).
The judge reads the final reply against these conditions and votes three times; two PASS votes pass the grader.

read.h: Run it several times, with and without
p: Ask Claude the same thing twice and you get two different answers. So one run of a case proves little: it can pass by luck or fail by luck. claude plugin eval runs every case three times by default. A run's score is the share of its graders that passed, weighted if you gave graders weights, and the case's score is the mean of its runs.

A high score still does not say that the skill helped, because Claude might do just as well without it. So each case is also run the same number of times with no plugin loaded. The two sets of runs are called the with-arm and the without-arm, the report shows both scores as WITH and W/OUT, and Δ (delta) is WITH minus W/OUT: what the plugin added. A Δ near zero means Claude does fine alone. A negative Δ means the skill made results worse, which is exactly what Dana's change did to small tickets.

One detail keeps the comparison fair. "The skill was loaded" can never pass without the plugin, so counting it would push every without-arm score down and make Δ look better than it is. In a two-arm run, a tool_used grader on Skill is therefore shown as an indicator, "the plugin fired", and left out of the score in both arms. When the whole point of a case is that the skill stays quiet, you add arm: both to that grader so it counts in both arms.
read.see:
CASE        WITH  W/OUT Δ      RUNS COST    NOTES
first-case  1.00  0.33  +0.67  6    $0.41

1 case(s) · mean Δ +0.67 · 74s · $0.41
(the summary claude plugin eval prints, from the docs)

deeper.h: Go deeper: when to trust a difference
p: Small suites are noisy. With 15 cases, one case changing its verdict moves the pass rate by almost 7 points, so a drop of one case means "run it again", not "the change is bad". That is why every case runs three times, why our scoreboard draws each pass rate with its spread (the gap between the best and worst of three rounds), and why a change counts only when it moves past that spread.

The command's exit code follows --threshold only: it exits 1 when any case's with-arm score is below it, 1.0 by default. Δ never changes the exit code, so a gate that cares about Δ reads it from the JSON result, aggregates.meanDelta, and fails the job itself.

read.h: Graders you can trust, cases the agent cannot see
p: Prefer free graders. A regex over the reply or a tool_used check costs nothing, gives the same verdict every time, and can run on every pull request. Use a judge only for what a pattern cannot see, such as "asks no questions", and write its criteria as concrete PASS and FAIL conditions. A judge can be wrong in ways that look convincing: a small judge model may fail a correct answer because it is formatted differently from what the criteria describe. So before a judge decides anything that matters, compare its verdicts with labels people wrote by hand on the same answers.

Give each skill at least one negative case, a request it must stay quiet on. A skill whose description fires on everything loads its body into sessions where it does not belong and steers Claude with instructions meant for another task, and only a negative case shows that.

The cases themselves are a golden set: fixed prompts with answers people confirmed, kept unchanged between the runs you compare. The agent under test must never see them, or it can learn the answers and score perfectly while proving nothing. claude plugin eval already hides the eval folder from the runs it starts; for our larger suites the cases live in a restricted repository the agents' tokens never reach.

lab.title: Score a skill with and without it, from recorded runs
needs: Claude Code 2.1.269 or later (claude --version), for claude plugin eval init
No model calls: the runs are recorded fixtures
lab.goal: Write an eval case for a small skill, then score six recorded runs with the case's own graders the way claude plugin eval does, and read WITH, W/OUT and Δ.

guess.q: With the welcome-note skill, 3 runs score 1.00, 1.00 and 0.50. Without it, 3 runs score 0.00, 0.50 and 1.00. What does the summary say?

options.text: WITH 0.83, W/OUT 0.50, Δ +0.33: the skill helps on this case
options.why: Each arm's score is the mean of its runs, and Δ is the difference. The best single run without the skill scored 1.00, which is why one run proves nothing.

options.text: WITH 1.00, W/OUT 1.00: both arms reached a perfect run, so no difference
options.why: The score is the mean over runs, not the best run. A skill that is right only sometimes scores lower.

options.text: The case fails, because one run with the skill scored 0.50
options.why: The case score is 0.83. Whether that passes depends on the threshold you set; Δ still says the skill helped.

solution.text:
# plugins/team-notes/evals/stays-quiet-on-goodbye/prompt.md
---
max_turns: 10
allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Skill]
tags: [pr]
---

Dana leaves the team on Friday. Can you write a short goodbye I can post in the team channel?

# plugins/team-notes/evals/stays-quiet-on-goodbye/graders/does-not-fire.md
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?welcome-note"'
min: 0
max: 0
arm: both
---

# plugins/team-notes/evals/stays-quiet-on-goodbye/graders/says-goodbye.md
---
type: regex
pattern: 'goodbye|farewell|last day|miss you'
flags: i
---

lab.fix: A teammate copied a grader from a Python project and wrote pattern: '(?i)goodbye|farewell|last day|miss you' without a flags line. Make the same change to says-goodbye.md and run the scorer: it stops with SyntaxError: Invalid regular expression … Invalid group. claude plugin eval uses JavaScript regular expressions too and does not support inline (?i). Fix the grader so it still ignores case, and run the scorer again.
explain: Why does every case run several times, and why with and without the plugin?
Why is a tool_used grader on Skill only an indicator in a two-arm run, and when do you add arm: both?
Which of your graders would you trust to run on every pull request, and which kind would you keep for a nightly run?
lab.done: You wrote a positive and a negative eval case, scored recorded runs of both, and can read WITH, W/OUT and Δ, including a negative Δ.

check.q: After a change to plan-and-grill, its suite shows every case above the 0.8 threshold, but the mean Δ is -0.12. Should the change ship?

options.text: Yes: every case passes the threshold
options.why: The threshold only says the results are good. Δ says they were better without the skill, so the skill now gets in the way.

options.text: No: on these tasks Claude does better without the skill than with it
options.why: A negative Δ means the skill makes results worse. Our gate fails the job on a negative mean Δ even when every case passes.

options.text: Yes, if the change also made the skill shorter
options.why: Shorter is good only when results hold. Here they got worse.

check.q: Why does a case run three times in each arm instead of once?

options.text: Because the first run warms up the model's cache
options.why: Runs are separate and isolated. The reason is that the answers differ from run to run.

options.text: Because the tool cannot grade a single run
options.why: It can; --runs 1 works for quick tries. It just tells you little.

options.text: Because a model answers differently each time, so one run can pass or fail by luck; the mean of several runs is a steadier score
options.why: In the lab the best run without the skill scored 1.00. Only the means showed that the skill helped.

check.q: Your case checks that welcome-note loaded, with a tool_used grader on Skill and no arm setting. In a two-arm run, how does that grader count?

options.text: It is shown as "the plugin fired" but left out of both arms' scores
options.why: It can never pass without the plugin, so counting it would make Δ look bigger than what the skill really adds.

options.text: It counts in both arms, like every other grader
options.why: Only with arm: both. By default a Skill grader is an indicator in a two-arm run.

options.text: It counts in the with-arm only
options.why: That would also inflate Δ. It is excluded from the score in both arms.

p: Every shared skill lives in a plugin in RhinoHealth/claude-plugins, and every skill comes with 3 to 10 eval cases in case.yaml form, at least one of them negative. Plugin CI runs claude plugin eval on each changed plugin. On a pull request it runs only the cases tagged pr, which use free graders; a nightly run at 02:23 runs every case of every plugin, judges included. The agent model is pinned to Opus 5.5 at medium effort and the judge to Sonnet 5.5, so a model rollout is never mistaken for a plugin regression, with --threshold 0.8 and --runs 3. A jq step fails the job when aggregates.meanDelta is below 0 and turns each case's negative Δ into a warning. The job runs on runners inside our cluster that reach the model only through the LLM gateway, so no Anthropic key sits on the runner; cost is reported and charted, with no ceiling until there are four weeks of data.

Skill evals are one of five suites. BYTE-GOLD scores Byte's reviews on past pull requests with known bugs, TICKET-BENCH runs Nova on 40 past fcp tickets with hidden tests, ROUTINE-BENCH scores each routine on past red builds and bugs, and BRAIN-QA asks the brain 60 real questions. Every suite runs each case three times, writes JSON to the eval results store, checks its judge against people's labels first, and keeps its golden set in a restricted repository with a leak check. The eval scoreboard in Grafana shows them side by side with their spread.

tickets.why: The eval gate in plugin CI: pinned models, pr-tagged cases on pull requests, all cases nightly, 0.8 and the negative-Δ check.
be-codebase's cases show the case.yaml shape, free graders on pull requests and a judge nightly.
Every task skill gets a negative case with min 0, max 0 and arm: both.
The eval results store: one JSON per run, turned into pass-rate, spread and cost series.
BRAIN-QA's golden set: real questions, source pages and answer points, kept where the bot cannot read them.

words.plain: A realistic prompt plus graders, kept fixed so runs can be compared over time.
One pass-or-fail check on a run: a regex on the reply, which tools were called, or a judge with criteria.
One side of the comparison: the runs with the plugin loaded, or the runs without it.
The with-plugin score minus the without-plugin score: what the plugin added. Negative means it made things worse.
A second model that grades a reply against written PASS and FAIL conditions; checked against people's labels before it is trusted.
Fixed cases with answers people confirmed, kept where the agent under test cannot read them.

review.q: Write a negative case for a skill of your own: the prompt, and the grader that proves the skill stayed quiet.
review.a: A realistic unrelated request, and a tool_used grader on Skill with input_match naming the skill, min 0, max 0 and arm: both.

review.q: A case scores 1.00 with and 1.00 without the plugin. What do you do?
review.a: Nothing is wrong, but the case does not show the skill's value: make the prompt test what the skill adds, or consider cutting that part of the skill.

review.q: Why do our pull-request runs use only regex and tool_used graders?
review.a: They are free and give the same verdict every time, so every pull request can run them. Judges cost model calls and vary, so they run nightly.

remember: Run each case several times with and without the skill, check results with free graders first, and trust the difference, not one good answer.
